title: HarborTask: a clearer repair queue
description: An original eight-slide startup pitch using an explicitly fictional shared-workshop service. All demand, pricing and pilot figures are illustrative assumptions.

slides.title: A repair request should become an owned next step
slides.body: Illustrative startup: HarborTask helps shared workshops turn scattered equipment requests into a visible queue, an assigned owner and a documented resolution. The initial audience is small workshop operators, not every maintenance team.
slides.notes: Open with a recognizable request arriving by email, paper and a corridor conversation. Replace HarborTask and the workshop segment with your venture. Describe a proposed service; do not present this example as a launched product.

slides.title: The problem sits between the messages
slides.body: In the worked scenario, a loose chair is reported three times while a broken light receives no owner. More messages do not create a reliable handoff. The job is to make responsibility and status clear.
slides.notes: Walk through the two requests in sequence. Replace these invented incidents with permissioned observations if available; otherwise keep them labeled as a scenario.
columns: Intake: requests arrive through several channels, with uneven detail.
Ownership: the next responsible person is unclear after a request is forwarded.
Closure: reporters cannot tell whether the issue was resolved or merely acknowledged.

slides.title: A small demand model makes the assumptions visible
slides.body: Illustrative weekly planning model: one shared workshop receives 18 requests, another 27 and another 35. These are invented workload examples used to discuss queue size, not customer research or evidence of market demand.
slides.notes: Explain what a request includes before comparing sites. Replace all three values with dated, attributable counts before using this slide as evidence. Do not multiply these examples into a market-size claim.

illustrativeChart.title: Illustrative requests per workshop per week
illustrativeChart.summary: The three invented workloads range from 18 to 35 weekly requests; this establishes a design range, not validated demand.

slides.title: One queue, three deliberate transitions
slides.body: The proposed workflow is simple: record the request with enough context, assign a responsible owner, then close it with a short resolution note. A visible waiting state explains when parts, access or specialist help are missing.
slides.notes: Use a single request to demonstrate each transition. Replace the example states with the minimum states your users actually need. Keep an ordinary task list as the comparison.
columns: Capture: location, issue, urgency and an optional approved image.
Assign: one accountable owner and a visible next update.
Resolve: record the action taken and tell the reporter what changed.

slides.title: Why this workflow instead of another inbox?
slides.body: The hypothesis is that a lightweight, shared queue can make ownership clearer than an inbox while requiring less setup than a full maintenance suite. The comparison below describes intended trade-offs, not tested superiority.
slides.notes: Invite scrutiny of the trade-off rather than declaring a winning product. Replace the alternatives and assumptions with a fair comparison relevant to the chosen segment.

illustrativeTable.caption: Illustrative workflow alternatives; assumptions to test
rows: Status and ownership may need manual conventions
A new habit and another tool to maintain

slides.title: A commercial hypothesis that can be disproved
slides.body: Example pilot offer: a six-week guided trial for one workshop, followed by a proposed flat site fee. The economic question is whether clearer handoffs create enough value to justify setup effort and the recurring fee.
slides.notes: Insert your real proposed offer and support effort. Keep price assumptions separate from signed contracts, willingness-to-pay evidence and recognized revenue.

illustrativeTable.caption: Illustrative offer assumptions, not sales or revenue
rows: Enough time to observe repeated use

slides.title: A pilot should test behavior, not collect compliments
slides.body: The proposed pilot follows one queue from intake to closure. Before it starts, agree how to measure owner assignment, stale requests and staff effort. Keep an exit option if maintaining the queue costs more attention than it saves.
slides.notes: Replace the suggested measures with a pilot agreement. Specify who records each measure and when the team will review it. Do not describe planned thresholds as achieved results.

slides.title: The ask: a bounded learning partnership
slides.body: Seek one workshop sponsor, one operational contact and permission to observe the existing handoff. The next decision is whether to run the six-week pilot; expansion depends on evidence from that pilot, not this illustrative demand model.
slides.notes: End with the exact commitment you need and a proposed review date. Replace role labels with consenting contacts and remove any request for access that your pilot does not require.

title: Northline Museum: a practical visit-planning redesign
description: An original client proposal for a fictional local museum. Scope, fees and schedule are editable illustrative planning examples rather than a real quotation.

slides.title: Help visitors plan a confident first visit
slides.body: Illustrative proposal: redesign Northline Museum’s visit-planning pages so a first-time visitor can find opening hours, accessibility information, travel options and ticket choices in one coherent journey.
slides.notes: Replace the museum and audience with the actual brief. Confirm the decision this proposal asks the client to make before discussing deliverables or fees.

slides.title: Start with the journey the site must support
slides.body: The worked scenario follows a visitor planning a Saturday outing with a child and a relative who needs step-free access. The site must answer practical questions before asking that visitor to choose a ticket.
slides.notes: Use this as a design scenario, not a claim about actual museum visitors. Replace it with a permissioned scenario from discovery, including access needs the client can reliably support.
columns: Can we visit? Hours, closures, access arrangements and support contacts.
Can we get there? Directions, transport choices and the entrance to use.
What do we book? Clear ticket options, conditions and the next action.

slides.title: A narrow scope makes delivery reviewable
slides.body: The proposed engagement covers the visit-planning journey and its supporting content. Collections search, membership systems and a complete visual rebrand stay outside this first engagement unless separately agreed.
slides.notes: Read the exclusions aloud. Replace them with the actual contractual scope and ask which dependencies could prevent launch. Do not imply third-party system work is included.
columns: Included: journey map, page structure, content guidance, responsive prototype and implementation support.
Outside this example: payment platform replacement, collection cataloguing, photography and a full brand redesign.

slides.title: Deliverables tied to decisions
slides.body: Each deliverable resolves a specific uncertainty. The team reviews the content structure before polishing screens and checks the working pages against agreed tasks before launch.
slides.notes: Replace owner roles and approval points with the client’s actual governance. Agree how feedback becomes one consolidated decision rather than a stream of incompatible requests.

illustrativeTable.caption: Illustrative deliverables and approval points
rows: Can the tasks be completed clearly?
Can the agreed design be built and maintained?
Are agreed tasks and content ready?

slides.title: A five-week route with visible dependencies
slides.body: Example schedule: discovery in week one, structure and content in week two, prototype review in week three, implementation support in week four and launch checks in week five. Client content and reviewer availability are dependencies.
slides.notes: Replace the weeks with a realistic calendar. Mark which tasks can overlap and who supplies access, source content and approvals. Treat late inputs as a schedule discussion, not an invisible assumption.

illustrativeTable.caption: Illustrative schedule; not a delivery commitment
rows: A decision on the proposed journey
Implementation access and web lead time

slides.title: Choose the support level deliberately
slides.body: Illustrative fixed-fee options compare a design-only handoff with a supported implementation. The higher option includes additional build review and launch support; neither includes third-party licences or an ongoing retainer.
slides.notes: Replace both amounts and inclusions with an authorized quotation. Explain taxes, payment terms and change control in the actual proposal documents rather than relying on this chart.

illustrativeChart.title: Illustrative engagement fees, example dollars
illustrativeChart.summary: The example design-only option is $8,000 and the supported implementation option is $12,000; these are invented planning values, not a quote.

slides.title: Resolve the risks before promising a launch
slides.body: The main uncertainties are content readiness, ticket-provider constraints and access to the current site. Confirm an owner and fallback for each. A clear manual route to visitor support is preferable to a broken booking or access-information link.
slides.notes: Use the client’s actual systems and access requirements. Replace generic risk statements with a specific dependency, impact and owner; agree escalation and change approval before work starts.

slides.title: The next decision and first working session
slides.body: Choose the engagement option, confirm the client project owner and agree the scope exclusions. The first working session should produce the visitor tasks, source-content inventory and review calendar needed to begin.
slides.notes: Close with the actual approval route and contact. Keep a written record of selected scope and assumptions; do not treat discussion during this presentation as a signed agreement.

title: Canopy portal migration: a decision-ready update
description: An eight-slide project update for an explicitly fictional internal service-portal migration. Status counts and dates are illustrative planning data.

slides.title: The migration is progressing; the access decision is open
slides.body: Illustrative status: Canopy’s internal service portal has completed content mapping and begun pilot migration. The next milestone depends on agreeing who approves access rules. This update separates completed work from the decision still needed.
slides.notes: Replace the project name, reporting date and status with current project evidence. State the requested decision early so the audience can interpret the detail that follows.

slides.title: What changed since the previous review
slides.body: In the worked example, the team finalized a page inventory, migrated a small pilot set and found conflicting access rules in the source system. The access issue is new information, not an unreported expansion of scope.
slides.notes: Name the source for each claimed completion and each new issue in a real update. Replace this scenario with actual changes; avoid presenting activity alone as delivery progress.
columns: Completed: agreed page inventory and migration rules for the pilot.
Learned: source permissions differ between two operating teams.
Needs a decision: one accountable approver for the target access model.

slides.title: Milestone progress against an explicit plan
slides.body: Illustrative checkpoint: discovery and content mapping are complete, the pilot is partially migrated and rollout has not begun. Counts describe accepted deliverables, not the percentage of all project effort finished.
slides.notes: Replace the work-unit definitions and all values with the current plan. Explain whether a count represents pages, acceptance checks or another unit before presenting the comparison.

illustrativeChart.title: Illustrative accepted work units at this checkpoint
illustrativeChart.summary: The example has reached its planned discovery and mapping counts, while pilot migration is 8 accepted units against 12 planned; rollout is not yet due.

slides.title: The remaining-work view is a forecast, not a promise
slides.body: This sample remaining-work line shows how the team might track a fixed pilot set over four weekly reviews. A slower reduction is a prompt to inspect blockers and scope, not evidence that individual staff are underperforming.
slides.notes: Replace the fictional values with a consistent work definition and show scope changes separately. Explain any acceptance bottleneck before treating the slope as a forecast.

illustrativeChart.title: Illustrative unaccepted pilot items by weekly review
illustrativeChart.summary: The sample remaining count falls from 24 to 10 over four reviews, with only two items accepted between reviews two and three.

slides.title: One issue requires leadership attention
slides.body: The pilot cannot close until conflicting access rules have an agreed owner. The proposed response is to pause only the affected pages, continue low-risk migration work and set a short deadline for the approval decision.
slides.notes: Replace the access example with the current blocking issue. Explain the consequence of waiting and the smallest decision that would release useful work; do not hide unresolved security questions behind a green status.

slides.title: The next fortnight has named outcomes
slides.body: The near-term plan is intentionally small: resolve access ownership, complete the pilot acceptance checks and prepare a reversible rollout rehearsal. Each outcome has a role responsible for reporting completion.
slides.notes: Replace roles with actual accountable people and relative timing with agreed dates. Confirm that owners accept the work before presenting the plan as committed.

slides.title: What would change the forecast?
slides.body: The worked forecast assumes no new source systems, a stable pilot scope and a reviewer available within two working days. If any assumption changes, the team will revise the milestone and explain the trade-off rather than compress checks silently.
slides.notes: Use assumptions the audience can verify. Replace the sample turnaround with the actual review agreement and identify the event that triggers a replanning conversation.

slides.title: Confirm the decision, then return to delivery
slides.body: Requested decision: appoint the access approver and confirm the pilot boundary. The next update should report the decision outcome, accepted pilot work and evidence from the rollback rehearsal, using the same definitions as this review.
slides.notes: Finish by recording the decision owner, due date and communication channel. Replace the next-update expectations with what the team can substantiate by that date.

title: Aster’s next quarter: focus before expansion
description: An original quarterly strategy deck for a fictional repairable desk-accessory retailer. Capacity allocations and targets are explicit illustrative choices.

slides.title: A quarter focused on dependable repeat purchase
slides.body: Illustrative strategy: Aster will spend the next quarter making its existing repairable desk-accessory range easier to understand, buy and support. A new product category is deferred until the core buying and support journey is more dependable.
slides.notes: Replace the retailer and strategic choice with your organization. State what will be postponed as clearly as what will be pursued; this example is not evidence of a real business outcome.

slides.title: The choice starts with constraints
slides.body: The fictional team has limited product, content and support capacity. Running a range expansion alongside checkout and support changes would create more work than the team can evaluate well. Focus is a capacity decision, not a claim that expansion has no value.
slides.notes: Replace these constraints with the real decision context. Distinguish a measured bottleneck from an assumption that still needs observation.

slides.title: Three priorities form one customer journey
slides.body: The priorities connect product understanding, a clear purchase decision and support after delivery. Work that does not improve one of these transitions needs an explicit reason to enter the quarter’s plan.
slides.notes: Use one example product to connect the priorities. Replace the actions with work your teams can own, and avoid turning the slide into a list of every department’s projects.
columns: Understand: explain material, repairability and product fit in plain language.
Choose: make compatibility, total price and delivery conditions clear.
Keep using: make spare parts, care guidance and support routes easy to find.

slides.title: Allocate capacity before promising initiatives
slides.body: Illustrative allocation of 100 planning units: 50 for the buying journey, 30 for post-purchase support and 20 for routine operation. These units are a planning convention, not a measured share of staff time or an approved budget.
slides.notes: Replace the total and allocation with an agreed capacity model. Include operational work rather than allocating every unit to new initiatives.

illustrativeChart.title: Illustrative quarterly capacity allocation
illustrativeChart.summary: Half of the example capacity supports the buying journey, 30% supports post-purchase improvements and 20% remains for routine operation.

slides.title: Each priority needs a testable outcome
slides.body: Define the signal before selecting the solution. In this example, the team will examine product-fit questions, checkout uncertainty and repeated care queries. The starting values must be measured before anyone sets a credible improvement target.
slides.notes: Replace each signal with a consistent definition and source. Do not fill missing baselines with invented historical data; assign baseline collection as real work.

illustrativeTable.caption: Illustrative outcome definitions; baselines still to measure
rows: Questions about product fit per reviewed order
Where task attempts stop or need help

slides.title: Sequence the work so learning can change it
slides.body: Begin with baseline collection and one product journey, then review that example before extending changes across the range. Reserve the final part of the quarter for checking the outcome and deciding what should continue.
slides.notes: Replace the relative sequence with a real calendar and dependencies. Identify the earliest review that could stop unnecessary work rather than waiting for a quarter-end presentation.
columns: First: establish definitions and work through one representative product.
Next: test the revised journey and extend only the useful changes.
Finally: review outcomes, support effort and the next quarter’s trade-offs.

slides.title: Stop rules protect the focus
slides.body: Pause expansion if support load rises beyond available coverage, the spare-parts story is incomplete or the buying changes create new confusion. Continue only when an owner can show what was learned and what will change next.
slides.notes: Replace the qualitative rules with agreed triggers where reliable measures exist. Assign a decision owner for stopping or redirecting work; a rule without ownership will not protect capacity.

slides.title: Approve the focus and its review rhythm
slides.body: The decision is to commit to the three connected priorities, protect operational capacity and defer range expansion. Review the evidence every month and record any change to priorities with its reason and capacity cost.
slides.notes: Close by confirming the accountable sponsor and first review date. Replace the fictional priorities and allocation before using this as an organizational strategy.

title: Cedar Station: a wayfinding case study
description: An original fictional design-portfolio example showing how to explain decisions and evaluation plans without inventing client results or user quotations.

slides.title: Cedar Station: make the next step understandable
slides.body: Illustrative portfolio case: redesign the information a first-time visitor needs when entering a small transit interchange. The brief focuses on finding the correct platform and understanding what to do when the route changes.
slides.notes: Replace the fictional station, project and role with your actual work. State whether the work was commissioned, personal or speculative; this example does not represent a real client engagement.

slides.title: Define the role and the boundary
slides.body: The example designer is responsible for the information hierarchy, sign prototypes and a task-based evaluation plan. Building work, live service information and operator policy are outside the design’s control and must be treated as dependencies.
slides.notes: Describe your actual contribution and collaborators without implying ownership of work done by others. Replace the boundaries with the constraints that shaped your decisions.
columns: Owned in the example: visitor-task definition, sign hierarchy and prototype decisions.
Dependencies: operator terminology, accessible routes, installation rules and accurate service information.

slides.title: Start with tasks, not a new visual style
slides.body: The proposed discovery plan follows three tasks: locate a platform, change between services and find assistance after a disruption. Existing signs, route choices and points of uncertainty would be documented before visual design begins.
slides.notes: Replace this planned method with the methods you actually used. Show permissioned artifacts where available; do not describe this fictional plan as completed user research.

slides.title: A worked journey reveals information gaps
slides.body: In the illustrative scenario, a visitor sees a platform number before learning which direction it serves. At the transfer point, the step-free route is unclear. These are designed examples of information gaps, not observations from real passengers.
slides.notes: Explain why each gap matters to completing the task. Replace the statements with traceable observations if you have them, preserving context rather than adding invented quotations.

illustrativeTable.caption: Illustrative journey gaps used to explain the design
rows: Show destination and direction before platform detail
Can I reach the next platform step-free?
Where can I get current help?

slides.title: A hierarchy that repeats at every decision point
slides.body: The proposed system presents destination first, route choice second and local detail last. Consistent wording and placement reduce the need to reinterpret each sign. Color supports the hierarchy but does not carry the route meaning alone.
slides.notes: Show a native diagram or your own approved prototype alongside this explanation. Replace the wording and colors with the actual system; describe the decision logic rather than relying on an attractive image.
columns: Primary: destination or direction in plain language.
Secondary: platform, transfer choice or accessible route.
Supporting: local identifiers and the next source of assistance.

slides.title: Show the decision, not an invented improvement claim
slides.body: The case study can compare what information is present before and after the proposed change. It cannot claim faster navigation or better accessibility without an appropriate evaluation. The example therefore reports design changes, not validated outcomes.
slides.notes: Replace the comparison with real artifacts you have permission to show. If you include an outcome later, name the method, sample, limitations and your role in producing it.

illustrativeTable.caption: Illustrative design comparison, not measured results
rows: Whether visitors choose the correct route
Whether the route is accurate and understandable
Whether visitors can reach useful help

slides.title: An evaluation plan matched to the task
slides.body: Test the prototype using realistic navigation tasks and a safe representation of the environment. Observe wrong turns, requests for help and interpretation of accessible-route cues. Record context and uncertainty alongside any timing measure.
slides.notes: Replace the plan with your completed evaluation if one exists. Arrange appropriate participation and permissions before testing; do not report planned observations as actual findings.

slides.title: What this case demonstrates
slides.body: The worked case demonstrates problem framing, a consistent information hierarchy and a plan to evaluate it. A next iteration would prioritize the most confusing decision point, then revise the system using observed task evidence.
slides.notes: Finish with your actual contribution, one limitation and one lesson you can substantiate. Add a real portfolio or prototype link only if you have permission to share it.

title: Small decisions, visible consequences
description: An original eight-slide event talk about practical decision records, illustrated by a fictional community-library equipment choice. No audience activity is required.

slides.title: The decision is small; the consequences still travel
slides.body: A community library needs a better way to lend equipment. The fictional team can buy a new checkout tool, simplify its current process or try a small manual pilot. The useful question is not which option sounds modern, but what the team needs to learn.
slides.notes: Open with the library scenario and make its fictional status explicit. Replace it with a story you can substantiate if appropriate. This talk can be delivered as a complete explanation without polling the audience.

slides.title: A hurried choice can hide three different questions
slides.body: In the worked story, one person wants less administration, another wants clearer availability and another worries about support. They appear to disagree about tools while actually optimizing for different outcomes.
slides.notes: Tell the story through the three concerns rather than inventing dialogue or quoting real people. Pause briefly so listeners can recognize the pattern in their own work.
columns: Outcome: what should become easier or more dependable?
Constraint: what must the solution respect?
Uncertainty: what do we need to learn before committing?

slides.title: Name a decision that someone can own
slides.body: A useful decision statement identifies the choice, the person accountable and the time boundary. In the example: choose how to run a four-week equipment-lending pilot, with the service coordinator owning the review.
slides.notes: Contrast this bounded decision with a vague instruction to modernize lending. Replace the owner role and time boundary with details appropriate to your own worked example.

slides.title: Compare options against the same questions
slides.body: The team compares three approaches using setup effort, ongoing attention and reversibility. The entries are illustrative judgments intended to expose assumptions; they are not a measured product comparison.
slides.notes: Walk through one row at a time. Explain that a low-effort pilot may still need disciplined records, and that a purchased tool does not remove operating responsibilities.

illustrativeTable.caption: Illustrative options for the library lending pilot
rows: Whether the workflow fits the service
Whether ambiguity is the main problem
Which information and controls are actually needed

slides.title: Make uncertainty a task, not a footnote
slides.body: The worked decision depends on two unknowns: how often availability is unclear and how much attention a new process would require. The team can investigate these with a short record of real lending tasks before making a larger commitment.
slides.notes: Replace these unknowns with the most consequential assumptions in your own story. Explain what observation would change the choice rather than adding more research without a decision purpose.

slides.title: A one-page record is enough to start
slides.body: Record the decision, alternatives considered, main reasons, owner and review date. Add the signal that would trigger reconsideration. This creates a useful memory of the choice without pretending that uncertainty has disappeared.
slides.notes: Read the example fields as a short narrative. Show how a later teammate could understand the reasoning without attending the original meeting.
columns: Decision and reason: try a bounded manual pilot to understand the workflow.
Owner and review: service coordinator reviews the pilot after four weeks.
Reconsideration signal: the process cannot be maintained or misses a critical service need.

slides.title: Does every small decision need this much attention?
slides.body: The amount of documentation should match the consequences and the cost of reversal. A routine, easily reversible choice may need only a brief note. A choice that changes access, money or shared responsibilities deserves a clearer record.
slides.notes: Acknowledge the cost of unnecessary process. Replace broad slogans with one example of a light record and one example that deserves more care; do not claim this approach has universal measured benefits.

slides.title: Leave the next decision easier to understand
slides.body: The practical takeaway is to name the outcome, expose the important uncertainty and record why the choice makes sense now. In the library example, the next step is a bounded pilot and an explicit review, not a claim that the final system has been found.
slides.notes: Close by inviting listeners to use the three questions privately on their next relevant decision. No response or platform activity is required. Replace the example with the one used consistently throughout your talk.

title: Mapline: follow a handoff from request to completion
description: An original product-demo story for a fictional handoff workspace. The proposed capabilities and sample records are illustrative, with no claims about a shipped product.

slides.title: One task, one visible outcome
slides.body: Illustrative product: Mapline is a proposed workspace for handing a recurring operational request from one team to another. This demo follows a fictional room-setup request until the requester can see what was completed and what remains open.
slides.notes: Replace Mapline and the task with your actual product and a sanitized demo record. Make clear which features are shipped, experimental or represented only by this example.

slides.title: Prepare a record the audience can follow
slides.body: The sample request is to prepare a meeting room for a small community event. It has a date, an accountable coordinator, a room contact and a short checklist. The demo uses fictional details and no personal attendee information.
slides.notes: Create the example record before presenting and verify permissions. If no product is available, explain the native diagram as a proposed workflow rather than imitating a working interface.

illustrativeTable.caption: Illustrative demo record
rows: Room layout and access checks confirmed
Checklist and a short resolution note

slides.title: Step one: capture enough context to act
slides.body: The requester records the intended outcome, timing and relevant constraints. The handoff should explain what success means, not merely attach a vague request title. In the example, room access and layout are explicit checklist items.
slides.notes: Demonstrate the actual fields in your product, or explain the proposed record if this remains a concept. Replace the constraints with details that are safe to show and relevant to the chosen audience.

slides.title: Step two: make the next owner visible
slides.body: The coordinator assigns the request to the room contact and adds the next expected update. The requester can distinguish an acknowledged request from work that has an owner. This is the central handoff to demonstrate.
slides.notes: Pause on the ownership transition. Show the real permission boundary and notification behavior if implemented; avoid claiming automation that the product does not provide.
columns: Before handoff: a request exists, but responsibility is not yet accepted.
After handoff: an accountable role and a next update are visible.

slides.title: Step three: show the exception path
slides.body: The fictional room contact discovers that one requested layout is unavailable. Instead of closing the request, the contact records the constraint, offers an alternative and returns the decision to the coordinator.
slides.notes: Use a harmless, predictable exception that demonstrates the real workflow. Explain where the product stops and a human decision begins. Do not hide the limitation behind an idealized success path.

slides.title: Completion should answer the original request
slides.body: The coordinator accepts the alternative layout and the contact records what was prepared. The completion note references the intended outcome and identifies any remaining task, so a closed status does not imply that every possible concern has disappeared.
slides.notes: Show the completed record and its history if your product supports them. Replace the sample resolution with one consistent with the exception shown on the previous slide.

slides.title: What this demo does and does not establish
slides.body: The scenario explains a proposed capture, ownership and closure flow. It does not establish integration coverage, security certification, delivery performance or customer results. Those claims need their own current evidence.
slides.notes: Replace this slide with accurate limitations and evidence links for your product. Be explicit about manual steps, supported roles and features unavailable in the demonstrated edition.

slides.title: Evaluate it with a task you actually need to hand off
slides.body: The useful next step is a bounded trial using a low-risk, representative request. Agree who will observe the handoff, what a successful outcome looks like and how the team will report friction before expanding use.
slides.notes: End with a real trial route or contact, not an invented customer story. Replace the trial scope with what your team can support and avoid requesting sensitive production data for a demonstration.

title: Wren Studio: your first useful week
description: An original onboarding deck for a fictional small service team. Role names, schedules and task examples are illustrative and editable.

slides.title: Your first week is about one useful contribution
slides.body: Illustrative team: Wren Studio helps local organizations improve everyday service information. In the first week, the goal is to understand how work moves, complete a supported task and know where to ask for help.
slides.notes: Replace the fictional team, purpose and first-week outcome. Explain what a newcomer is not expected to know yet, and confirm that the example reflects the actual role.

slides.title: How work moves through the team
slides.body: A request becomes a short brief, then a small piece of work, a review and a recorded handoff. The team makes questions visible early so the person receiving the work can understand what is ready and what still needs a decision.
slides.notes: Walk through one real, permissioned example if available. Replace the stages with the team’s actual workflow and identify where the newcomer can find the current status.
columns: Understand the brief: outcome, audience and constraints.
Make a useful first version: small enough for timely feedback.
Review and hand off: record the decision and the remaining work.

slides.title: A first-week plan with room for support
slides.body: The sample week moves from access and context toward one supported task. It is a guide, not a requirement to complete work before essential access or assistance is available.
slides.notes: Replace the days and owner roles with an agreed plan for the actual newcomer. Adjust for role, working hours, access needs and prior experience.

illustrativeTable.caption: Illustrative first-week plan
rows: Know the team purpose and support contacts
Find the tools and a model brief
Review what helped and choose the next task

slides.title: Access is a prerequisite, not a test
slides.body: The newcomer needs the agreed communication channel, project workspace and example materials before starting the task. Missing access should be reported through the named support route rather than worked around by sharing another person’s account.
slides.notes: Replace the generic tools and support route with the actual approved setup. Confirm access before assigning delivery expectations; do not include passwords, access tokens or private customer material in this deck.

slides.title: A worked first task: clarify a service notice
slides.body: The example task is to rewrite a fictional room-booking notice so readers can find who may book, what information is needed and how to ask a question. The output is a short draft plus a note explaining any unresolved uncertainty.
slides.notes: Use a real low-risk task and an approved example of acceptable work. Keep the first attempt small enough for useful feedback; replace the fictional notice before assigning the task.

slides.title: What a useful review looks for
slides.body: The review checks whether the reader can understand the next step, whether the content is accurate and whether assumptions are visible. Feedback should identify a concrete change and its reason, rather than simply asking for a more polished tone.
slides.notes: Show one example of specific feedback from materials you can share. Replace the criteria with the team’s actual standard and explain who can approve factual changes.
columns: Clarity: the intended reader can find the next action.
Accuracy: claims and instructions match approved source information.
Handoff: the reviewer can see open questions and the next owner.

slides.title: Where to go when the next step is unclear
slides.body: Ask the task reviewer about the work, the onboarding partner about team routines and the designated support contact about access. If the person you need is unavailable, use the agreed escalation route instead of waiting without an update.
slides.notes: Replace every role with a current contact or maintained directory link. Confirm permission before adding personal contact information; do not leave fictional contacts in a delivered onboarding deck.

slides.title: Close the week with a clear next step
slides.body: The end-of-week conversation reviews the completed task, unresolved questions and the support needed next. A useful outcome is one agreed next task and one improvement to the onboarding plan, rather than a claim that onboarding is finished.
slides.notes: Set an actual check-in time and invite private feedback. Replace the sample next step with a task suitable for the person’s responsibilities and available support.

title: From booking friction to a small service experiment
description: An original worked workshop deck using a fictional community-room booking service. The full explanation works without required polls or platform activities.

slides.title: Leave with one experiment the service can actually run
slides.body: Illustrative workshop: a community centre wants to reduce confusion during room booking. The output is one bounded change, a responsible owner and a way to learn whether the change makes the next step clearer.
slides.notes: Replace the service and output with the workshop brief. This deck includes a complete worked example; optional discussion or practice can be added in the notes without making an activity necessary to follow the story.

slides.title: A shared scenario keeps the discussion concrete
slides.body: In the fictional example, a volunteer requests a room, receives an acknowledgement and waits for confirmation without knowing whether more information is needed. Staff see an incomplete request but have no consistent follow-up message.
slides.notes: Read the scenario neutrally and avoid assigning blame. Replace it with a permissioned example or keep it explicitly illustrative; do not imply that the scenario was observed at a real centre.

slides.title: Map the handoff before proposing a new tool
slides.body: A simple service blueprint separates what the requester sees from the work happening behind the scenes. This exposes the point where an acknowledgement can be mistaken for a confirmed booking.
slides.notes: Explain each column using the same request. If you invite optional practice, give participants the same boundaries and enough context to avoid guessing about the service.

illustrativeTable.caption: Illustrative booking-service blueprint
rows: A message that the form arrived
Update the schedule and notify the requester

slides.title: The friction is a missing distinction
slides.body: The worked map suggests that receipt and confirmation look too similar to the requester. A new platform is one possible response, but a clearer message and visible next step are smaller changes the team can test first.
slides.notes: Distinguish the map’s hypothesis from a verified cause. Replace it with the uncertainty your evidence supports, and avoid treating the first suggested solution as the only option.

slides.title: Turn the hypothesis into a small experiment
slides.body: The example experiment rewrites the acknowledgement to say that the request was received but is not yet confirmed. It states what happens next, when to expect an update and how to provide missing information.
slides.notes: Use approved service facts when drafting the real message. If the promised response time cannot be met consistently, change the process or the wording before the experiment begins.
columns: Change: distinguish receipt from confirmation in one message.
Learn: whether requesters can explain the current status and next step.
Boundary: one booking channel during a short, agreed review period.

slides.title: Choose evidence that matches the question
slides.body: The team can walk through the revised message with representative task scenarios and review clarification requests during the pilot. Completion counts alone would not reveal whether people understood the booking status.
slides.notes: Replace the proposed observations with a practical, permissioned evaluation plan. Establish how notes will be recorded and keep personal information out of the workshop artifacts.

slides.title: Plan for the constraints that could undo the change
slides.body: The message needs an owner, accurate service conditions and a maintained support route. If staff cannot deliver the stated next step, the team must revise the promise or stop the pilot rather than publish reassuring but inaccurate copy.
slides.notes: Assign real owner roles and a review date. Optional group practice can use the worked example, but the presenter should still explain the completed plan for anyone who does not participate.

slides.title: A finished workshop leaves an owned decision
slides.body: The worked decision is to test one clearer acknowledgement, keep the original available for comparison and review the evidence before expanding. Record the owner, start date, review date and the signal that would stop or change the experiment.
slides.notes: Replace the sample decision with the actual workshop outcome. Read back the commitment and identify who will maintain the record after the session; do not equate agreement in the room with implemented change.

title: A change is not yet an explanation
description: An original lesson on comparisons and causal claims using explicitly invented library reminder examples. It is complete without required questions or scored activities.

slides.title: What can a before-and-after comparison tell us?
slides.body: Suppose a fictional library introduces a reminder and the share of books returned on time rises. The change is worth investigating, but the before-and-after numbers alone do not establish what caused it.
slides.notes: Introduce the difference between describing a change and explaining it. State that the library and every value in the lesson are invented for teaching; no real intervention result is being reported.

slides.title: First describe the change accurately
slides.body: Illustrative values: 60% of books were returned on time in one period and 75% in the next. The increase is 15 percentage points. That calculation describes the difference between the two percentages, not the reminder’s causal effect.
slides.notes: Show 75 minus 60 explicitly. Distinguish percentage points from a relative percentage change, and replace these values only if the same definitions are used in both periods.

illustrativeChart.title: Illustrative on-time return percentages
illustrativeChart.summary: The invented on-time return rate rises from 60% before the reminder to 75% afterward, a difference of 15 percentage points; causation has not been established.

slides.title: Ask what else could have changed
slides.body: The later period might include different borrowers, a different mix of books or a holiday that changes return behavior. A measurement rule might also have changed. Each possibility offers another explanation for the observed difference.
slides.notes: Use the alternatives to show why a plausible story is not the same as evidence. Do not claim that any one alternative actually occurred in the fictional example.
columns: People: were the same kinds of borrowers included?
Context: did timing, borrowing patterns or other services change?
Measurement: were on-time returns defined and recorded in the same way?

slides.title: A comparison group adds useful context
slides.body: Imagine a second, comparable branch without the new reminder. Its change over the same period can help reveal whether a wider trend may be involved. Comparability remains an assumption to investigate, not a fact guaranteed by adding a second row.
slides.notes: Explain why the same time window matters. The table is another invented example; do not present the difference between changes as an established causal estimate without considering the design and its assumptions.

illustrativeTable.caption: Illustrative comparison; no causal conclusion is established

slides.title: Plan the study around the claim you want to make
slides.body: A stronger study decides how to assign or compare reminder conditions, define the outcome and handle missing records before examining the result. Where feasible, random assignment can help reduce systematic differences between conditions.
slides.notes: Keep the explanation at the level appropriate to the audience. Clarify that implementation, sample size and analysis still matter; naming random assignment does not make every study definitive.

slides.title: Report the boundary as part of the result
slides.body: Even a useful study may apply only to the included borrowers, the tested message and the period observed. A claim about all libraries or permanent behavior change would require additional evidence.
slides.notes: Show how a precise limitation makes a result more useful rather than less interesting. Replace the fictional boundaries with the actual design before discussing a real study.
columns: Who: the people and settings actually included.
What: the exact reminder and outcome measured.
When: the observed period and the duration still unknown.

slides.title: Choose wording that matches the evidence
slides.body: With only the original before-and-after values, a careful statement is that on-time returns increased after the reminder was introduced. Saying the reminder caused the full increase makes a stronger claim than that comparison supports.
slides.notes: Read the two statements aloud and identify the extra causal claim. Do not introduce a required quiz; a presenter can explain the distinction directly.

illustrativeTable.caption: Illustrative claims and their evidential scope
rows: On-time returns increased from 60% to 75% after introduction
The reminder caused the entire increase
A causal explanation requiring stronger support
The reminder will improve returns everywhere
A broad generalization requiring additional evidence

slides.title: A reusable habit: describe, compare, qualify
slides.body: Describe exactly what changed, ask what comparison supports the explanation and state the boundary of the conclusion. These steps help readers distinguish an interesting observation from a causal claim and an overextended generalization.
slides.notes: Close by revisiting the opening example in these three steps. Optional private reflection can use another everyday claim, but the lesson remains complete without an audience response.

title: Field notes offline: an illustrative research readout
description: An original research-readout rehearsal using a synthetic field-note workflow dataset. No interviews, customers, participants or validated findings are invented as real evidence.

slides.title: The decision: what must an offline note preserve?
slides.body: Illustrative research readout: a team is exploring a field-note tool used where connectivity is unreliable. This deck rehearses how to present evidence and uncertainty using synthetic task records; it does not report completed research.
slides.notes: Replace the fictional context and synthetic records with traceable, permissioned evidence before presenting real findings. State the product decision the actual research is meant to inform.

slides.title: Separate the research plan from the evidence in hand
slides.body: The example plan would observe note capture, interruption and reconnection tasks. For this rehearsal, only scripted task records exist. They can test the reporting structure but cannot establish user needs, prevalence or product effectiveness.
slides.notes: Explain the difference between a planned method and completed work. Replace this inventory with actual sources, collection dates, consent constraints and limitations; never relabel synthetic rows as interviews.

illustrativeTable.caption: Evidence inventory for this synthetic readout
rows: What the team proposes to examine
Whether the reporting structure is coherent
No participant finding can be claimed
No prevalence or outcome claim can be made

slides.title: A worked coding view makes interpretation inspectable
slides.body: The synthetic records are grouped by where the workflow becomes uncertain: whether a note was saved, whether an attachment is available and whether a reconnect duplicates work. The labels describe the example scripts, not themes discovered from people.
slides.notes: Replace the coding with your documented analysis process and link it to permitted source material. Preserve disagreements or ambiguous cases rather than forcing every record into a neat category.

illustrativeTable.caption: Illustrative coding of scripted workflow issues
rows: Can the author tell what is retained?
An image is not yet available offline
A reconnect repeats a pending action
Is one accepted action recorded once?

slides.title: Counts should explain their denominator
slides.body: In the twelve synthetic task records, eight follow the intended path and four encounter a scripted interruption. These counts describe a rehearsal dataset. They are not a success rate from user testing and should not be used as one.
slides.notes: Replace both the counts and denominator with real evidence if available, and retain context about task selection. Do not convert this synthetic proportion into a customer-performance claim.

illustrativeChart.title: Synthetic task-record outcomes; not participant results
illustrativeChart.summary: Eight of twelve invented task records follow the intended path and four contain scripted interruptions; the chart illustrates reporting structure only.

slides.title: Three design hypotheses to investigate
slides.body: The worked analysis suggests making retained state visible, distinguishing local from synchronized content and explaining pending work after reconnection. These are hypotheses derived from the scenario, not validated research recommendations.
slides.notes: Replace each hypothesis with a finding-to-design link you can substantiate. Explain what observation would challenge it, and avoid presenting a synthetic theme as a quote from a customer.
columns: Retained state: the author can tell what is safely stored locally.
Synchronization state: the interface distinguishes local and shared versions.
Recovery state: pending work has an understandable next step.

slides.title: What this readout cannot answer
slides.body: The rehearsal cannot determine how often interruptions occur, which people need offline capture or whether the proposed status language is understandable. Those questions need appropriate research in the intended settings.
slides.notes: Use the limitations to prioritize the next study, not merely as a disclaimer at the end. Replace the questions with the unresolved decisions in your actual project.

slides.title: Turn hypotheses into a focused evaluation
slides.body: A next study could test whether people can identify saved, pending and synchronized states during realistic interruptions. Begin with clear tasks and a documented recovery path; record misunderstanding and context alongside completion.
slides.notes: Replace the proposed study with an approved plan, appropriate participants and a feasible recruitment route. Assign ownership for preserving source evidence and reporting uncertainty.

illustrativeTable.caption: Illustrative next-study questions
rows: Can someone identify a locally saved note?
Their explanation after a scripted interruption
Can they resume without duplicate work?

slides.title: A useful readout makes the next evidence request clear
slides.body: The worked recommendation is to investigate state comprehension before expanding features. The next review should show actual source-backed observations, which hypotheses changed and the product decision those observations support.
slides.notes: Replace this rehearsal conclusion after real research. End with the decision owner, planned evidence and review date; remove synthetic charts from any presentation claiming validated findings.

title: Community print room: repair, replace or share?
description: An original decision brief for a fictional arts centre considering its print-room workflow. Costs, volumes and trade-offs are illustrative and must be replaced before any real purchase decision.

slides.title: Choose a dependable print-room route
slides.body: Illustrative decision: a community arts centre must choose whether to repair its current printer, replace it or use a nearby shared service. The aim is dependable access for routine materials within the centre’s operating capacity.
slides.notes: Replace the centre, equipment and decision boundary. Make clear that the example is a planning exercise, not procurement advice or a recommendation about a real product.

slides.title: Agree the criteria before comparing prices
slides.body: The worked brief considers availability, total operating effort, expected cost and the ability to change course. A low purchase price alone would not answer whether staff can maintain the service or whether members can use it when needed.
slides.notes: Replace these criteria with the centre’s actual requirements and approval process. Identify any mandatory access, support or compatibility condition before applying preference scores.
columns: Service fit: availability, access and the tasks the centre must support.
Operating fit: staff effort, supplies and support responsibilities.
Decision fit: affordability, uncertainty and the cost of reversal.

slides.title: Three options, with explicit boundaries
slides.body: Repair keeps the existing workflow but depends on a reliable service assessment. Replacement changes equipment and may require setup. A shared service reduces equipment responsibility but introduces travel, scheduling and external-service dependencies.
slides.notes: Replace the generic options with verified, comparable offers. State which tasks each option includes and excludes; do not assume an external service is continuously available.

slides.title: Compare like-for-like planning assumptions
slides.body: The illustrative first-year figures include an initial action and expected operating costs. They exclude taxes and any unlisted facility changes. They are invented to demonstrate the comparison and are not vendor quotations.
slides.notes: Replace every amount with an authorized, dated source and use the same period and task scope. Do not rely on this example for a real spending decision.

illustrativeTable.caption: Illustrative first-year example costs, not quotations

slides.title: Operating attention is a separate comparison
slides.body: In the worked model, repair requires more monthly staff attention than replacement, while the shared service requires coordination time. These invented estimates help expose a trade-off that a cost-only table would miss.
slides.notes: Replace the hours with a defensible estimate or measured task record. Explain what work is included, and avoid treating a forecast as an observed saving.

illustrativeChart.title: Illustrative monthly staff hours by option
illustrativeChart.summary: The example allocates 4 monthly staff hours to repair, 2 to replacement and 3 to coordinating a shared service; none is a measured operational result.

slides.title: Ask which uncertainty could reverse the choice
slides.body: The repair option changes substantially if the service assessment cannot support the expected use. Replacement changes if setup or supply costs rise. The shared option changes if opening hours or turnaround cannot meet the centre’s needs.
slides.notes: Replace the uncertainties with the largest decision-sensitive assumptions in actual offers. Gather the missing evidence before refining small differences in estimated cost.

illustrativeTable.caption: Illustrative decision-sensitive uncertainties
rows: Whether the fault and expected service life are understood
Whether setup and ongoing supplies are included
Written service conditions and a task trial

slides.title: A conditional recommendation is more honest than a forced winner
slides.body: For the worked scenario, investigate repair first only if a credible assessment supports the required use and support effort. Keep replacement and the shared service as explicit alternatives if that condition fails. This is a decision rule, not a claim that repair is best.
slides.notes: Replace the rule with the actual owner’s justified recommendation. State the evidence that would change it, and do not present this fictional example as a purchase recommendation.

slides.title: Approve the next evidence step and its owner
slides.body: The immediate decision is to authorize a bounded assessment and collect comparable operating information. Record who will obtain it, the spending authority required and the date for returning with a final recommendation.
slides.notes: Replace owner roles, approval limits and dates with the actual process. Close by confirming the next decision, not by implying that an equipment purchase has already been approved.
